title: A next-word machine
prompt:
Build the counting part of a next-word machine.

`count_pairs(notes)` returns a dictionary of dictionaries: for each word, how many times each other word came right after it. `most_likely(counts, word)` returns the most common next word, or `None` when the word never had a next word.

When it works, `python3 nextword.py` guesses that *rattles* comes after *fan*.
hints: Split each note into words. Pair each word with the one after it: `zip(words, words[1:])`.
For each pair, make sure `counts[first]` exists (`setdefault` helps), then add 1 to `counts[first][second]`.
In `most_likely`, fetch `counts.get(word)`. If it is empty, return `None`. Otherwise `max(options, key=options.get)`.
explain_after: A language model predicts the next word from the words before it [ml-087]. Your machine looks back only one word. That is the n-gram idea: approximate a word's probability from the last few words instead of its whole history [ml-088]. The decoding choices Jurafsky and Martin describe include greedy decoding and random sampling [ml-091]. Our machine always takes the top word, and in Code Pix we call that the greedy choice.
